name: Flight of the Woodcock
short_description:
The Eurasian woodcock (Scolopax rusticola) is a migratory forest bird, widespread from northern Europe to Central Asia, wintering in temperate regions. It stands out for its extraordinarily precise cryptic plumage — an intricate mosaic of rufous, brown, and beige streaked with black that makes it virtually invisible in the underbrush. Its long, straight bill, sensitive at the tip, is an instrument for probing moist soil; its large dark eyes, set high and toward the back of the skull, give it an almost circular field of vision — the bird sees what is behind it while probing ahead.

The diagonal composition was chosen to capture the raw energy of the woodcock’s takeoff: the bird erupts from the bottom of the painting, wings spread in a vigorous upward beat, its head turned back as if stealing one last glance before flight. It is the takeoff that reveals the woodcock in all its graphic complexity: on the ground, it does not exist — it vanishes into the leaf litter; in the air, every feather is exposed. The background of warm ochre washes and splatters, crossed by a few blue-gray strokes, evokes the golden light of an autumn forest without weighing down the composition.
description:
The Eurasian woodcock (Scolopax rusticola) is a discreet and mysterious migratory bird, emblematic of the dense undergrowth of Europe and Asia. It stands out for its perfectly camouflaged plumage, a true marquetry of brown, fawn and grey, as well as for its long sensitive bill and its large dark eyes set very high on the head, giving it an exceptional 360-degree field of vision.

The vertical composition was chosen precisely to highlight the upward movement and energy of its take-off. The bird occupies the centre of the painting, its rounded wings pointed upwards in the abrupt beat so characteristic of the species. It is flight that reveals the woodcock in all its liveliness and breaks its invisibility: on the ground, it blends completely into the leaf litter; in the air, it unveils all the graphic complexity of its feathers. The background of warm ochre splashes and washes brings out the subtle tones of its woodland plumage without weighing down the composition.

description:
The red fox (Vulpes vulpes) is the most widespread wild canid in Europe, found from deep forests to the edges of cultivated fields. Opportunistic and cunning, it hunts alone at dawn or dusk, guided by remarkably sharp hearing that allows it to locate prey from a distance. The brown hare (Lepus europaeus), a dweller of open plains, is among its emblematic prey: its speed and unpredictable zigzags nonetheless make it a formidable opponent, one the fox can only surprise through a patient approach.

The fox is shown standing on an old stump rendered in graphite, its catch held firmly in its jaws. The composition focuses everything on the gaze: the amber eyes, fixed on the viewer, betray neither triumph nor violence — only the quiet fulfilment of the predator. The blazing red of the coat contrasts with the muted brown of the hare, while the background of warm ochre and blue-grey washes strips the scene of all context to keep only the essential: a moment of wild life, without judgement.

description:
Kimya means 'peace' in Swahili. It is the word that comes to mind when I look at this leopard. Not the stillness of an absence of danger — the peace of the sovereign predator, who has nothing to prove, nothing to demonstrate. He is simply there, and that is enough.

I built the entire composition around the gaze. Nothing else was permitted to take precedence — the coat, the background, everything is arranged to draw the eye back to those eyes. Steady, direct, without aggression. A gaze that neither flees nor attacks.

The background tones are deliberately soft, almost neutral. I wanted nothing to compete with the precision of the coat and the depth of that gaze. The light is gentle, even — it envelops without dramatising. That is a rare choice for me, accustomed as I am to strong contrasts.

Kimya is an invitation to slow down. To look without fear. To understand that serenity can exist in the eyes of a predator.

description:
Today, as I paint this tiger, my thoughts go to that little boy, barely born, who is at this very moment undergoing open-heart surgery on the other side of the Atlantic. I cannot help but see him as a small tiger fighting for his life.

When I paint, my thoughts and the moments I am living become forever bound to each brushstroke. It is as though I were pinning small moments of life to the canvas, and together they form a larger pattern that makes sense.

This charging Bengal tiger — fixed gaze, unshakeable stride — became, without my deciding it, the portrait of a force both raw and fragile. The force that moves forward when everyone else is afraid. His paws raising the dust, his golden eyes that do not blink: it is the same energy as that small fighter on his operating table.

'Heart of Oak' — it is what we say of someone who does not bend. This little man and his first great battle will be forever bound to this painting, as we all pray for him and his family. His name is Oakland Sledge.

The American bison is a living fortress. When it moves through snow, it is not the bison that yields — it is the storm.

'Snowpiercer' — the title came to me as an obvious choice, like that film which left its mark on me: a train that never stops, that drives through ice and cold because stopping would mean death. This bison does not flee winter, it charges straight through it. It does not go around. It pierces.

description:
The equinox is that fleeting moment when night and day are of equal length. The choice of the zebra imposed itself as the natural way to illustrate this duality. Its stripes are not mere patterns; they are a graphic score in which black and white confront and complete one another. In "Equinox", this interplay of lines creates a visual dynamic.
The canvas's balance is also played out in a confrontation of chromatic temperatures. By choosing to reveal only part of the animal's "face", I move beyond simple naturalistic representation and enter another dimension: the frontal gaze is the central pivot — an invitation to introspection, creating a direct and almost mystical bond between the observer and the wild. description:
To paint the woodcock is, for me, an attempt to hold one's breath. Those who walk the autumn woods know that cardiac lurch when the 'belle' bursts from underfoot.

In this painting, I did not want to paint a bird, but the pure adrenaline of the encounter. The bird is caught in full flight, the tail feathers spread and the bill pointing along its line of escape.

The composition of the painting rests on a balance between force and dynamism. The tree trunk on the left, with its gold-leafed branches, serves as a solid, vertical anchor. It creates a natural frame that literally projects the bird into the empty space on the right. This diagonal of flight, initiated by the movement of the wings and extended by the woodcock's long bill, gives an immediate sensation of speed.

The vivid, almost electric yellow of the beech leaves in the foreground contrasts with the cold, muted blue of the mist that envelops the forest. This palette of grey-blues and faded mauves in the background is not merely an aesthetic choice: it symbolises the space of freedom into which the bird is about to vanish. The light strikes the top of the wing like a piece of sky.

The woodcock is here only a silhouette in passing. The title evokes both its success in escaping our gaze and the luck we have, as observers, to seize that fraction of a second. This is not only the portrait of an animal — it is the portrait of a moment that has already ceased to exist by the time we look at it.

description:
This painting was born from a fascination with the quiet power of the Alpine ibex, a creature whose robust silhouette stands out with singular force in the most austere of environments. My intention was to capture that moment when the animal seems to merge with the mountain — a presence at once tangible and almost evanescent in the veil of mist.

The composition is organised around the ibex as its central figure, whose imposing horns and attentive posture immediately captivate the eye. I sought to convey the raw texture of its coat, contrasting with the immaterial softness of the mist that partially envelops it. This mist is not simply a background; it actively participates in the atmosphere of the work, creating a sense of depth and mystery while concentrating attention on the animal.

The chosen tones, dominated by ranges of grey, white, and muted brown, aim to evoke the coldness and mineral quality of the alpine landscape in winter. The light, subtly diffuse, models the forms and underscores the sculptural presence of the ibex, lending it an aura of serenity and contained strength. The sole bright point at the centre of the painting is its orange eye.

I orchestrated the planes with care. In the foreground, touches of winter vegetation emerge timidly from the snow, anchoring the scene in tangible reality. Then the eye rises towards the ibex, whose fur, worked with meticulous attention to detail, contrasts with the elusive softness of the mist around it. In the background, rocky masses can be made out — ghostly forms sculpted by time and the elements, adding depth and silent texture to the whole.

Through this portrait, I wished to pay tribute to the resilience and wild beauty of this emblematic animal. It is an attempt to capture a moment of contemplation, where nature reveals itself in its grandeur and its fragility. My hope is that this image might prompt in the viewer an emotional connection with the natural world, and an appreciation for the discreet majesty of the Alpine ibex in its habitat.

description:
"The Sanctum" — Oil painting — Gorilla in the jungle.

In 'The Sanctum', my artistic intention was to create a vision in which the jungle becomes a timeless sanctuary, a sacred place beyond the reach of mankind's destructive hands. The gorilla, majestic and powerful, stands as a guardian — the silent protector of this virgin, preserved space. It symbolises the strength and ancestral wisdom of nature, embodying the role of keeper of the secrets and mysteries buried in the depths of this forest. The painting invites the viewer to connect with nature in all its wild splendour, and to recognise the beauty and fragility of this threatened world.

The composition of 'The Sanctum' is organised around the gorilla, which occupies a central place and becomes the focal point of the work. It is slightly off-centre, creating a visual dynamic that guides the viewer's gaze through the dense jungle vegetation. The massive trees and lush plants frame the scene, forming a natural arch that evokes the idea of a gateway to a hidden kingdom. The light filtering through the foliage creates a luminous path — an invitation to explore this wild land. The gorilla's position, with its broad shoulders and intense gaze, reinforces its protective role, while the background dissolves into a subtle mist, suggesting the immensity and mystery of this jungle.

The atmosphere is at once mystical and soothing, with a palette dominated by deep greens, blue-greys, and touches of golden light. The dark, saturated tones of the foliage create a sense of thickness and depth, making the humidity of the forest almost palpable. Rays of soft light, piercing through the canopy, bring a feeling of calm and serenity while highlighting the gorilla's silver coat — a symbol of wisdom and mature age. The diffuse mist in the background adds a touch of mystery, suggesting that this sanctuary extends far beyond what the eye can perceive. Together, these elements create an introspective, almost spiritual atmosphere, inviting the viewer to lose themselves in the meanders of this sacred jungle and to feel the profound bond that unites us with nature.

The creation of "Damanius" is far more than an exercise in artistic technique; it is a profound tribute to the raw power and fragility of the black rhinoceros, an ancient species now threatened with extinction. Since childhood, this animal has fascinated me, embodying at once indomitable strength and a poignant vulnerability in the face of the dangers of the modern world.

The palette — from vermillion reds to ultramarine blues — brings its features to life, while the contrast between warmth and cold underscores the duality of its existence: power and survival against oblivion.

Painting Damanius was a total immersion, almost meditative. For weeks, I lived at the rhythm of its contours, obsessed by every detail, every imagined movement. As the painting came to life, it fixed its gaze on me, imposing a presence at once imposing and melancholy. This silent interaction between artist and subject symbolises the urgency of preserving what is precious and fragile.

"Damanius", whose name means "The Untameable", is far more than a portrait. It is a reminder, a silent cry for the protection of this threatened giant. description:
The bongo (Tragelaphus eurycerus) is one of the largest antelopes of the tropical forest.

I spent two weeks deep in the tropical forest of Cameroon in search of this majestic, colourful, wild, and shy antelope. Two days' drive from the nearest town, the rainforest of central Africa is the world's second largest forest massif, spanning five countries: Cameroon, Gabon, the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the Central African Republic.

What strikes you first is the extreme humidity and density of this forest. As soon as you pass through the wall of vegetation that borders the tracks, you enter a world apart — made of sounds, smells, and sensations never encountered before. This is no longer the Africa I know; it is something else. And this is only the beginning of a sensory experience that will first fill me with wonder, then terrify me, and finally exhaust and wring me out.

What I wanted to convey in this painting is ultimately that incredible experience I lived. The main subject of the painting is, in the end, less the bongo than this forest that grabs you, drawing you into its labyrinth of elephant-made tracks. The composition guides the viewer's eye; mystery carries you along; you are inside the painting, and the only way out is that source of light.

description:
This painting holds a special place for me, as I have a fascination with the roe deer that is as great as it is inexplicable. It seems to me that this animal is one of those beings fashioned directly by the divine: its elegance, its posture, the way it holds its head, its trophy — everything about it commands admiration. It is like a melody without a false note.

Since childhood, every time I see a roe deer at the edge of a road or round a bend in a path, I feel the same delight, never jaded. I must have inherited this from my grandfather, who, the moment he spotted a roe deer emerging from the wood, would stop whatever he was doing, move closer to the window, and contemplate this furtive apparition until it vanished.

description:
The first encounter with a lion is a moment that marks you for life. Whether on a photographic safari or a hunt, crossing the gaze of the king of the savanna leaves no one unscathed.

With each new painting, I ask myself: what is the purpose of this piece, what message will I convey, what emotion do I want to transmit?

I firmly believe that we all carry within us the memory of our ancestors — an instinct for survival, a hunter's instinct, that gives us this ancestral fear of the predator. I am transfixed by the lion; I feel a primal fear mingled with fascination, and that is precisely what I want to convey in this painting. I want to create a silent dialogue between man and beast, to find in its gaze that unreasoning dread.

I wish to give my representation of the lion in all its majesty and savagery. The image of the ultimate predator — it must be at once beautiful and menacing. This duality is found in the opposition between warm tones and cool tones. The composition is raw, essential: a portrait, without embellishment, in chiaroscuro. The gaze is piercing; one must lose oneself in it and be unable to escape.

In the end, I detail more precisely the eyes, the muzzle, and the jaws. The rest of the head loses focus in order to capture the viewer's gaze all the more.

The title of this painting is "Maximus", superlative of Magnus in Latin, meaning the greatest.

description:
The Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep is one of two species of wild sheep in North America — and the most immediately recognisable. Those horns that curl in on themselves over the years, that can weigh up to 14 kg — as much as the rest of its skeleton. Not like a trophy — like a sculpture. It is absurd. It is magnificent.

I wanted to make a close, frontal portrait that offers no escape. The background is neutral, almost abstract — all the space is his, for those horns that invade the frame. The cold mountain light models the volumes with an almost mineral precision, each groove telling a year of life, a winter weathered in the scree of the Rockies.

There is also an unexpected story in this painting. The bighorn is no longer endangered today — not despite hunters, but partly because of them. The collaboration between hunters and conservationists has enabled the formation of conservation groups that ensure the species remains abundant. That is the complexity I love in nature: nothing is simple, everything is connected.

BigHorn. A name that says exactly what you see: those great horns, and behind them, the calm eye of an animal that has all the time in the world.

description:
Wildlife artist Stéphane Alsac presents here his latest painting: the portrait of the celebrated female leopard of the Masai Mara — Romi.

My first encounter with Romi goes back several years. Having observed a good number of leopards, I must say she exerts a certain fascination — and clearly not only on me. Indeed, each leopard is different, and Romi is one of those panthers who have a certain indefinable 'something more'. She is beautiful.

This time, it has now been several months since Romi disappeared. It is not the first time she has remained so impossible to find, and I think I am going to have to leave Kenya without having seen her. After several days of fruitless searching across her vast territory, my guide announces that she has finally reappeared and left a kill in a tree on the edge of a river.

She is sure to return in the evening to take a few morsels from her prey. We take up position and after an hour's wait, as though she had prepared her entrance, she appears. I am breathless; I know this will last only a few minutes, so I shoot: she poses, stretches against the tree, takes flight, then disappears into the foliage.

In the end, it is my son who got the finest image — the one I will use for this painting, a tribute to the Queen of Leopards.

description:

'Razzle Dazzle': the English expression for a noisy and confusing situation. It is also the name given to American ships from the First World War, painted in highly contrasting oblique patterns — directly inspired by the natural camouflage of zebras. The idea was not to conceal them, but to make any estimation of their heading and speed impossible.

That is exactly what I felt finding myself in the middle of the Great Migration in Kenya. Thousands of zebras in motion, a compact mass of crossing, overlapping, blurring black-and-white stripes. The eye seeks a line, an individual, a direction — and finds only movement.

In this large-format work, I wanted to place the viewer where the predator stands: face to face with this living camouflage, searching in the mass for the most vulnerable individuals. In this painting, there are three calves. Can you find them?

But it would be wise not to be deceived by their condition. These monoliths are known to put up a fierce fight when frightened, wounded, or cornered, even pursuing potential threats such as lions. They were notoriously difficult to bring down, which is why they were included in the 'Big Five'.

When I painted this work, it was that duality that guided me: old age and power, solitude and menace. This buffalo is alone, marked by the years — hide cracked, gaze heavy — but there is something in its posture that clearly says it has not had its last word.

description:
There is in the Nile crocodile an economy of means that commands respect. Motionless for hours, sometimes days — then a tenth of a second. That is all. The prey never saw it coming. A valve at the back of the jaw closes at the moment of plunging, preventing it from drowning with its victim. It can then go without eating for up to a year, even two for the oldest. This is not patience — it is indifference to time.

In 'Jaws', I wanted the viewer to feel the threat physically. The composition uses a wide-angle effect — the viewpoint is at the animal's level, very close, which distorts the perspective and makes the jaws appear disproportionate to the rest of the body. They literally emerge from the painting, almost in relief. You are within jaw range. And you know that in a tenth of a second, it is over.

To render the scales of the Nile crocodile, I abandoned my usual technique and returned to the Dutch masters: successive layers of transparent glazes, applied patiently. It is this method that gives the scales their iridescent reflections, that blend of yellows and greens that appears alive in different lights. A slow, meditative way of painting — ultimately in the image of this animal that has made immobility a weapon.

description:
The Derby eland is a mythical animal, and encountering it leaves a mark. It has even become a passion for some. Such is the case for my client who commissioned this painting.

It was in his company that I set out on the trail of the Derby eland in the Faro reserve in Cameroon. Taurotragus derbianus is the largest antelope in Africa and is today classified as 'vulnerable'. Little known to the general public and far from the superficial concerns of armchair ecologists, it owes its survival in the wild today solely to the relentless fight against poaching carried out and financed by conservationist hunting companies.

It took long hours of walking, more than ten days in all, to have the chance to observe the 'Ghost' — as it is also known. For the Derby eland does not allow itself to be approached easily; the females, standing sentinel, watch from every direction, and the slightest sound or scent sends them galloping away, putting an extra two to three hours' walking between us.

In the end, I wished to immortalise in this painting, first and foremost, the fleeting vision of this elegant Giant glimpsed between the trees of a heavily wooded savanna. Then I tried to convey the atmosphere of end of day, at the close of an exhausting day of tracking — a moment of almost unreal magic. Finally, I hope this painting transmits the excitement and emotion that were mine in that intense moment when I encountered the 'Lord Eland'.

For me, the title of a painting must evoke something special — a story, an emotion underlying the contemplation of the work. This evocation may be immediate for the viewer, or more discreet, even mysterious.

Often a title comes to me during the work itself, like something obvious, evoking something very personal that I share only with my client, like a secret. Other times it takes longer — and it may take longer than the painting itself. It becomes then a collective naming, which I find very pleasing.

'Aoskway' means moose in Huron, the celebrated Native American people of North America who have hunted it for centuries. It is a little like the spirit of the valiant Huron hunter that lives on in this Aoskway.

I wanted to convey an impression of power and grace. The elk advances with a quiet authority — massive, sovereign, as though bearing the weight of its territory. description:
In the mist, there is always that moment before. Before the bear sees you, before it makes up its mind, before it disappears. I wanted to paint that silence — a British Columbia grizzly moving through the cold morning water, the world still suspended between night and day.

The North American grizzly is one of the most impressive creatures on the continent. In British Columbia, it lives in river valleys and coastal forests — where the salmon run, where water and forest meet. It moves with a deceptive slowness, that particular rolling of the shoulder that speaks at once of power and ease. In the early morning, when mist still covers the banks, it is often the only living creature visible in the landscape. The world belongs to it.

For this painting, I chose a background completely dissolved — no forest, no mountain, no context. Nothing but the mist, the water, and the animal. The horizontal composition widens the space, giving the bear the room it actually occupies. I framed low, at water level, so the viewer is at the animal's level — not above it, with it. The raised paw fixes the instant: a step, an intention, a presence.

The muted palette — whites, warm greys, deep browns — says something that cannot quite be named. The grizzly does not threaten. It crosses. And it carries with it something of the world before.

description:
The Great Migration is one of the most breathtaking spectacles in the animal world. Hundreds of thousands of zebras and wildebeest in motion, driven by instinct and the need to find fresh grass on the other side of the Mara River. The crossing — the moment the herd plunges into the water — is the tipping point of the entire migration.

A single zebra is enough to trigger the movement. A moment of collective hesitation, then the mass surges forward. The crocodiles wait, motionless below the surface. Within minutes, thousands of animals cross at the same point in a chaos of hooves, water, and dust. I witnessed this moment. You do not forget it.

The composition is deliberately destabilising — like a badly framed photograph taken in the melee. The zebras climb the opposite bank, seen from behind: a rare perspective, almost abstract, in which the black-and-white stripes interweave in motion. No central figure, no hierarchy — just the mass in movement, the bank rising, and the energy of a headlong rush.

My intention was to freeze a moment of pure chaos. Not the crossing in its entirety, but this fragment — noisy, imperfect, overflowing the frame. Something that gives the viewer the impression of having been there, in the wrong place, at the right moment.

description:
In a lion pride, it is the females who form the heart of the group. They are the ones who raise the cubs, who organise the hunt, who maintain the bonds. The males orbit around them, absent themselves, return — never very far, but rarely at the centre. The Mayambula Pride, observed in the Timbavati in South Africa, functions like all prides: according to immutable rites passed from generation to generation without being taught.

Drinking in the late afternoon is one of them. That moment marks the transition between two times: the heat falling, the cubs about to start playing, the females who may set out to hunt. Lionesses and cubs side by side, at the same height, in the same light — an ordinary scene of life that, seen close up, has something unforgettable about it.

I positioned myself at their level. This choice determines everything: you enter the scene, you are no longer a spectator. The composition is organised around a horizontal line of gazes — mothers and cubs intermingled, each eye a slightly different colour. The light of the golden hour falls diagonally from the right, sculpting the fur textures in dense contrasts. Working these textures at length, the painting tips almost into abstraction — and yet the scene remains profoundly familiar.

What I wanted to capture is this paradox: something absolutely wild that resembles a family scene. Those eyes looking at you without seeing you, that intimacy you are witness to without being invited. The Golden Hour is perhaps the painting in which I have most felt that boundary between the animal world and something we recognise as our own.

description:
I have always associated the tiger with fire. Perhaps since childhood, since The Jungle Book and Shere Khan — that big cat that Mowgli faces with torches, as though fire were the only answer to its power. Perhaps also simply because of its coat: that burnt-orange background crossed by black flames, that alternation of warmth and darkness that resembles embers in motion. The Bengal tiger is not an animal like any other — it is an apparition.

Emeraude du Bengale was born of this long-held fascination. I wanted to paint the royal tiger in all its verticality, its whole body in the frame, at the moment it drinks — an instant of suspension, a grace almost contradictory with what it represents.

The composition is vertical, Japanese in spirit: flat areas of colour, simplified motifs, an economy of form that concentrates all attention on the stripes. These black flames on an orange background become the subject of the painting as much as the animal itself. The palette narrows, the details fade away — and this paring back reveals something almost abstract, graphic.

With this painting, I wanted to move away from strict naturalism towards something more graphic, more deliberate in its stylisation. Not less faithful — differently faithful. Faithful to what the tiger evokes rather than to what it is.

description:
"Do not give ground… hold fast… flee, then return, charge again… do not give ground!!"

This Cape buffalo is worn down, exhausted by the relentless attacks of the African wild dogs — these painted dogs that hunt in packs. It is certainly stronger than them, but encircled by the 'painted wolves', it will tire until it can no longer hold, until it can no longer fight. In the meantime, it must not give ground.

There is a paradox in this scene that I love: the African wild dog, the 'painted hunting dog', is one of the most endangered animals in Africa. Fewer than 3,000 individuals. Considered a nuisance, it is poisoned by farmers. A formidable predator on one hand, an endangered species on the other. Nature does not distribute roles simply.

I built this composition around tension and movement. The buffalo occupies the centre, a dark and massive presence, surrounded by wild dogs pulling from every direction. The main diagonal creates a sense of vortex, of pressure that leaves no escape. The dust, the light, the bodies off-balance — everything is designed so that the eye finds no rest, exactly as the buffalo finds no respite.

What interested me was to paint not the predator nor the prey, but the moment between the two — resistance. This buffalo may have no chance. But it charges. It comes back. It does not give ground. There is in that obstinacy something universal, that goes far beyond the animal world.

description:
Africa is not short of grand stories or dramas — the big cats, the migrations, the endless ballet of predators and prey. But there are also small stories, carried by protagonists one does not always notice. With this painting, I wanted to set aside the great African stage and focus on an encounter between two minute actors.

On one side, a dung beetle pushing its fortune backwards — one of the rare animals known to navigate by the Milky Way. On the other, a leopard tortoise advancing in a straight line, without stopping, unaware of the dangers around it. Unaware, too, of the presence of this small beetle. It takes its name from the spots on its shell that evoke the rosettes of the great cat — each groove tells a year spent on this earth, and some live more than a century. They are heading in opposite directions. And a tiny pebble, in the wrong place, could trap them both in a face-to-face whose outcome is unknown.

To tell this story, I chose to get down to their level — as though one were lying on one's belly in the bush dust, or suddenly shrunk to their scale. This viewpoint creates an unexpected intimacy: the tortoise and the dung beetle become the only inhabitants of this world, and their encounter, the central event.

Each carries its burden — the tortoise, its shell; the beetle, its ball. Two parallel equilibria, two worlds that should never have crossed, united by the chance of a path and the threat of a pebble. We do not know what is going to happen. And perhaps that is 'une question d'équilibre' — this suspension between two destinies that ignore and brush past each other.

description:
Between the lion cub and the lion, grace does not disappear — it transforms into majesty. At this age, everything is still open — curiosity prevails over wariness, and those golden eyes look at the world without yet knowing that they will end up making it their domain. In every clumsy movement, every yawn too large for its still-small mouth, the predator it will become is already visible.

The title imposed itself naturally. Not only because this cub is the son of a king — but because it embodies something universal that Saint-Exupéry captured so well: that way of being fully present, without calculation or defence, of seeing the world with fresh eyes. Lion cubs, like children, have not yet learned to pretend.

For the composition, I chose to approach as closely as possible. The tight framing is no accident: I wanted us to be face to face with it, almost at the level of its gaze, unable to avoid that presence. No distancing, no savanna as a backdrop — just it, that gaze, and that fur, still soft, that has not yet taken on its definitive colour.

Oil paint, worked in the hyperrealist tradition, attaches itself here to seizing the infinite nuances of this ochre and tawny coat, the light playing on the small, still-uncertain tufts, this transitional mantle between childhood and the majesty to come. To paint Le Petit Prince was to fix the pre-reign — that suspended, fragile, and unrepeatable moment when a future king still observes the world with a child's eyes.

description:
The leopard is the only great cat that hoists its prey into trees. A behaviour that is equal parts genius and obsession — to keep for oneself, safe from hyenas and lions, what one has spent hours hunting. Watching this scene, the title imposed itself naturally: Mon Précieux. Not as a joke — as a truth.

In the savanna, the leopard is an exception: solitary where lions live in prides, discreet where cheetahs run in the open. This individuality extends to its way of hunting — and of keeping. What it conquers belongs entirely to it, without sharing or concession. Mon Précieux is also a portrait of character: that of an animal that has never learned to share.

For the composition, I chose a low angle: we look upward, as though standing at the foot of the tree. The leopard dominates the frame, suspended between sky and earth, its prey hanging in the void. This verticality was essential — it speaks of ascent, of effort, and of that way the leopard has of placing its quarry out of reach of the world.

The light filtered through the foliage creates a play of golden spots on the dappled coat — two patterns that echo and almost merge with each other. Oil paint, in its capacity to graduate values with infinite precision, is the ideal tool for seizing this chromatic complexity: the beige, the ochre, the black of the rosettes, and that African light that traverses everything.

There is something universal in this scene — and profoundly funny. A father who would very much like to rest after the hunt, and two cubs who have other plans. The nap of the king of animals will not happen: his lion cubs have decided he is a playground. The title, I must say, did not come from me: it was found by the person who now owns this painting — and no one could have said it better.

For the composition, I opted for a triangular structure whose line of force runs from the lion's mane to the left paw of the cub — a diagonal that concentrates the energy of the scene. The father's reaction — mouth half open, oblique glance — animates what might have been merely a tranquil end-of-day scene. It is this tipping point between rest and chaos that captivated me.

The painting plays on a near-monochrome — ochre, tawny, beige dominate, barely contrasted by the blue shadows of the declining light. It is the lion's head that catches the eye: lit from the front, it emerges from the background in a contrast of warm and cool tones that oil paint renders with great precision.

What I love about this painting is that it says something true about family life — among lions as elsewhere. Majesty does not long resist two determined cubs. And in that resignation of the father, halfway between irritation and tenderness, I recognise something very human.

description:
The English expression 'high and mighty' describes the quiet arrogance of those who have nothing to prove. Facing a charging elephant, it takes on a radically different meaning — and a much more urgent one. Tusks pointing forward, trunk raised, the entire mass launched in your direction: you understand immediately what high and mighty really mean.

An elephant's first charge is often a mock charge — a show of force, not a real attack. The rule in the field is simple: do not move. Simple to state. Much harder to apply when several tonnes are heading straight at you. It takes a considerable amount of composure — and a reading of animal behaviour that one trusts with eyes closed.

For the composition, I chose a ground-level viewpoint — as though one were directly in the line of charge. The raised trunk, the tusks forward, the mass occupying the entire frame: nothing is left at rest in this image. I wanted the viewer to feel the pressure of this instant, the compressed air between the elephant and us.

Oil paint gives all its density to that rough and living skin, those deep folds where the light fractures, that texture which alone speaks of age and power. The hyperrealist work seeks here to capture not only the form — but the tension of this suspended instant between intimidation and flight.

description:
The African buffalo (Syncerus caffer) is one of the animals most feared by African hunters. Its memory is legendary: a wounded buffalo can ambush its pursuer hours later. The power of its head — dominated by the 'boss', the massive horn-base that fuses the two horns together across the skull — is unmatched among the ungulates.

Here, no body, no staging — just the face of the buffalo filling the frame. The eyes half-sunk beneath the boss, the ridged muzzle, the unruly ears. One must look long at this head to read anything in it — and that is precisely the challenge: to find expression in a face that nothing predisposes to expressivity.

description:
Kenya, Masai Mara, fourth day of safari. For the first time, I had brought my two children with me — those who had watched me paint lions all their lives, but who had never seen one in the wild. That day, we came upon this superb male who had just killed a wildebeest. He stood up to hide his prey in a thicket, turned back — and planted his eyes in mine. No aggression. Just a look that said it all: I’ve got my eye on you.

To do justice to that moment, there was only one way: to paint the lion at full size. A direct confrontation, no distancing possible. The lion occupies the entire format, frontal gaze, the prey still in his mouth. The tight framing leaves no escape: you are in the scene.

Oil paint allows here a precision that borders on the documentary — every nuance of the African light, every hair of the mane still in the movement of rising, every detail of the wildebeest in the mouth — while remaining a painting. It is that tension between raw reality and the artistic act that hyperrealist work seeks.

This painting sometimes provokes incomprehension — even rejection. Viewers have reproached me for painting a scene of violence. That reaction says something about our times: a society increasingly disconnected from the living, that forgets that hunting for food is as old as life itself. I am not here to tell a reassuring story — neither Bambi nor The Lion King. I paint life as it is, with its moments of grace and its dramatic moments. That lion’s gaze, I wanted it frontal and unequivocal: because truth deserves to be looked straight in the face.
